belief: My spouse should make me happy.
origins: Romantic stories may suggest that finding the right spouse ends loneliness and unhappiness. Growing up with little comfort can leave you longing for a partner who will finally meet every need. Stress, disappointment, or losing touch with friends and interests can make your marriage carry more of your emotional life than one relationship can hold.
teaches: Marriage is meant to include love, care, companionship, and shared responsibility. Wanting affection and fair treatment is reasonable. But a spouse cannot provide lasting happiness at every moment or meet every emotional need. Scripture honors marriage while also pointing us toward God, wise relationships, and our own daily choices. The guidance in Pearls calls us to treat others as we wish to be treated and to speak gently. Taking responsibility for some sources of joy does not excuse a spouse’s neglect or harmful behavior.
self_statements: If I feel unhappy, my spouse is failing me.
I should not have to find enjoyment outside our time together.
A good spouse would always make me feel special.
My mood depends entirely on what my spouse does.
If marriage takes work, something must be wrong.
My needs matter, so my spouse should meet all of them.
errors: Turning a reasonable wish for care into a demand for constant happiness.
Giving another person complete responsibility for your emotional life.
Judging the marriage as bad whenever you feel unhappy.
Noticing disappointments while overlooking care, support, or other sources of meaning.
questions: What care can I reasonably ask of my spouse, and what am I asking one person to provide alone?
Have I clearly asked for the specific behavior I want?
Have I ever felt unhappy even when my spouse was caring?
Which friendships, activities, habits, or spiritual practices support my well-being?
Can I appreciate love without requiring my spouse to manage every feeling?
What is one step I can take today without waiting for my spouse to change?
truth: I can expect love, respect, and effort in my marriage without expecting my spouse to keep me happy all the time. My feelings have many influences. I can ask clearly for care, contribute to our relationship, and build joy through God, friendships, meaningful activities, and healthy daily habits.
hw_truths: I can ask for care without demanding constant happiness.
My spouse matters deeply, but is not my only source of meaning.
I can take one helpful step for my well-being today.
Love includes mutual effort and realistic expectations.
My needs deserve clear, respectful words.
Disappointment does not erase every good part of our marriage.
log: Record one caring interaction, one action you took for yourself, and your mood before and after. Include disappointments honestly.
actions: Beforehand, predict your enjoyment from 0–10. Spend 20 minutes on it and record your actual enjoyment.
At a calm time, ask for something doable, such as ten minutes together without phones. Record the response without treating it as a verdict on your worth.
Arrange a brief call or walk. Notice whether support can come from more than one relationship.
Offer one small act of care freely.
Choose something you can give without using it as a test or demanding an immediate return.
prayer: Father, thank You for the gift of companionship and for Your love that reaches beyond any one relationship. Help me ask honestly for care, love my spouse wisely, and take responsibility for the steps I can take toward a meaningful life. Amen.
meta: Christian belief counseling for “My spouse should make me happy.” with BSB scriptures, questions, songs, and practical homework.

name_example: Sarah can practice being quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
